The words were first printed, unsigned, as 'Battle Hymn of the Republic' in The Atlantic Monthly, vol. IX, no. LII, February 1862, p. 145 (evidence ia-atlantic-1862-02-leaf0-p145.jpg). Julia Ward Howe died on 17 October 1910 (loc-naf-howe-n50029084.marcxml.xml).

The tune was in print by 1859 as the hymn 'Say, Brothers, Will You Meet Us?': the American Sunday-School Union's Prayer-Meeting Tune-Book credits it only to an arranger, 'A. T.' (ia-prayer-meeting-tune-book-1859-p105-n110.jpg), and Jenks's Devotional Melodies prints it the same year, arranged by E. P. Resteen (ia-jenks-devotional-melodies-1859-p59-n64.jpg). An 1858 printing is reported at second hand only.

The tune's composer is unknown, and this receipt records the composer as unknown. The Library of Congress enters the song under its title and cites Fuld: none of the claims to its composition can be sustained (loc-naf-battle-hymn-no00005966.marcxml.xml).

Claimants, none of them recorded as the author. William Steffe is the most-cited: the Library of Congress gives his dates as approximately 1830-1890 (loc-naf-steffe-nr95043969.marcxml.xml), and a William Steffe of Philadelphia died in 1911 (ia-grand-lodge-pa-1911-djvu.txt), but whether he is the same man is not established. The Library of Congress also names Thomas Brigham Bishop (1835-1905) and Frank E. Jerome, and an 1861 Boston edition credits Phillip Simonds (loc-john-browns-song-1861-simonds-item-2023783905.json).

The work as a whole was first published in 1862, with the words; the tune's own first publication, 1859, is earlier. The licence predicate reads 1862 for both of its rules, and a later year can only refuse more. An anonymous work's EU term runs 70 years from its publication (Directive 2006/116/EC, Art. 1(3): legislation-gov-uk-eudr-2006-116-art1.html).

The source edition is Battle Hymn of the Republic, Boston: Oliver Ditson & Co., 1862, plate 21454, deposited on 9 April 1862 (loc-ditson-1862-item-2023782802.json, loc-ditson-1862-muscivilwar-200000858-001.jp2). Its music pages name no composer or arranger (loc-ditson-1862-muscivilwar-200000858-002.jp2), so its harmonisation is by an unknown hand. Its introduction and verse accompaniment already appear in Ditson's July 1861 'Glory, Hallelujah', also anonymous (loc-glory-glory-1861-ditson-item-2023783074.json).
Quotes from .jpg and .jp2 evidence were read from the image by the archivist, and the SHA-256 pins the image that was read. Bracketed text in them is the archivist's description, not print.
This project dedicates the arrangement to the public domain under CC0 1.0, which its LilyPond file states. The file's header names si-jam-sessions as the arranger, as the brief asked.
